summary.text: Choose the least \(K\) with \(n^2\le K^3\) and take all integers up to \(K\) together with all primes up to \(n\); for each \(m\le n\), its largest divisor \(d\le K\) has complementary factor \(m/d\) either at most \(K\) or prime, since otherwise its least prime factor and the maximality of \(d\) would force \((K+1)^3\le n^2\), a contradiction. A central-binomial-coefficient argument gives \(n\le(\log_2 n+1)(\pi(n)+1)\), which together with \((\log_2 n+1)^3\le8n\) yields \(K\le2(\pi(n)+1)\); hence the covering set has at most \(K+\pi(n)\le5\pi(n)\) elements.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_n=\{1,2,\ldots,n\},
\qquad
S\cdot S=\{xy:x,y\in S\}.
\]
For \(n\ge 1\), let \(a(n)\) be the minimum cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq T_n\) such that \(T_n\subseteq S\cdot S\). This minimum exists: \(T_n\) itself is admissible, since \(1\in T_n\) and every \(x\in T_n\) is \(x\cdot1\). We prove the stronger explicit estimate
\[
a(n)\le 5\pi(n)\qquad(n\ge2),
\]
where \(\pi(n)\) is the number of primes at most \(n\). The desired boundedness then follows with constant \(5\).

We first establish the numerical estimate that will control the size of the covering set.

### 1. A prime-counting estimate

We will prove that, for every integer \(N\ge2\),
\[
N^2\le 8\bigl(\pi(N)+1\bigr)^3. \tag{1}
\]

We begin with a standard central-binomial-coefficient argument, including the needed details.

#### Central binomial coefficient bounds

For \(m\ge1\), put
\[
B_m=\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
We claim that
\[
B_m\le (2m)^{\pi(2m)}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, write the prime factorization of \(B_m\) as
\[
B_m=\prod_{p\le2m}p^{v_p(B_m)}.
\]
For each prime \(p\), one has
\[
p^{v_p\binom{r}{s}}\le r \qquad(0\le s\le r,\ r>0). \tag{3}
\]
Here is an elementary justification. Legendre's formula, obtained by counting the multiples of \(p,p^2,\ldots\) among the factors of a factorial, gives
\[
v_p\binom{r}{s}
 =\sum_{j\ge1}\left(
 \left\lfloor\frac r{p^j}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac s{p^j}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{r-s}{p^j}\right\rfloor
 \right).
\]
Each parenthesized term is either \(0\) or \(1\), because for real numbers \(u,v\),
\(\lfloor u+v\rfloor-\lfloor u\rfloor-\lfloor v\rfloor\in\{0,1\}\). It vanishes when \(p^j>r\). Consequently
\[
v_p\binom{r}{s}\le \lfloor\log_p r\rfloor,
\]
and hence (3) follows. Applying (3) with \(r=2m\) and \(s=m\), every prime-power contribution \(p^{v_p(B_m)}\) is at most \(2m\). There are exactly \(\pi(2m)\) relevant primes, proving (2).

We also need the lower bound
\[
4^m<mB_m\qquad(m\ge4). \tag{4}
\]
This follows by induction. At \(m=4\), \(B_4=\binom84=70\), so
\(4^4=256<280=4B_4\). The factorial formula for binomial coefficients gives the recurrence
\[
(m+1)B_{m+1}=2(2m+1)B_m. \tag{5}
\]
If \(4^m<mB_m\), then
\[
4^{m+1}<4mB_m\le 2(2m+1)B_m=(m+1)B_{m+1},
\]
which proves (4) for all \(m\ge4\).

Now suppose \(N\ge8\), and set \(m=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\). Then \(m\ge4\), \(2m\le N\), \(m\le N\), and \(N-1\le2m\). Monotonicity of \(\pi\), together with (2), gives
\[
B_m\le(2m)^{\pi(2m)}\le N^{\pi(N)}.
\]
Combining this with (4), we obtain
\[
2^{N-1}\le 2^{2m}=4^m
 <mB_m
 \le N\,N^{\pi(N)}
 =N^{\pi(N)+1}. \tag{6}
\]

Let
\[
L=\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor,
\]
so that
\[
2^L\le N<2^{L+1}.
\]
It follows from (6) that
\[
2^{N-1}<N^{\pi(N)+1}
 <\bigl(2^{L+1}\bigr)^{\pi(N)+1}
 =2^{(L+1)(\pi(N)+1)}.
\]
Since powers of \(2\) are strictly increasing, this implies
\[
N-1<(L+1)(\pi(N)+1).
\]
Both sides are integers, and therefore
\[
N\le (L+1)(\pi(N)+1) \qquad(N\ge8). \tag{7}
\]
This is the Chebyshev-type estimate needed below.

#### Controlling the logarithmic factor

For every integer \(k\ge0\),
\[
(k+1)^3\le2^{k+3}. \tag{8}
\]
For completeness, this can be proved by induction. The initial cases needed at the start of the induction are immediate. For the inductive step, once \(k\ge3\), expansion gives
\[
(k+2)^3\le2(k+1)^3;
\]
indeed the difference between the right and left sides is
\(k^3-6k-6\), which is nonnegative for \(k\ge3\). Thus, if
\((k+1)^3\le2^{k+3}\), then
\[
(k+2)^3\le2(k+1)^3\le2^{k+4}.
\]
The cases before \(k=3\) are checked directly, proving (8).

Applying (8) to \(k=L\), and using \(2^L\le N\), gives
\[
(L+1)^3\le2^{L+3}=8\cdot2^L\le8N. \tag{9}
\]

We can now prove (1). First suppose \(N\ge8\). Set
\[
A=L+1,\qquad B=\pi(N)+1.
\]
By (7), \(N\le AB\), while (9) says \(A^3\le8N\). Consequently
\[
A^3\le8N\le8AB.
\]
Since \(A>0\), cancellation gives
\[
A^2\le8B.
\]
Therefore
\[
N^2\le A^2B^2\le8B^3
 =8\bigl(\pi(N)+1\bigr)^3,
\]
as required.

It remains to cover \(2\le N<8\). Since the prime \(2\) is counted, \(\pi(N)\ge1\), and hence
\[
8(\pi(N)+1)^3\ge8\cdot2^3=64.
\]
On the other hand \(N\le7\), so \(N^2\le49<64\). Thus (1) holds for every \(N\ge2\).

### 2. Construction of the covering set

Fix \(n\ge2\). Let \(K\) be the least positive integer satisfying
\[
n^2\le K^3. \tag{10}
\]
Such an integer exists because \(K=n\) works: as \(n\ge1\), \(n^2\le n^3\). In particular,
\[
1\le K\le n. \tag{11}
\]
Define
\[
S=S(n,K)=\{1,2,\ldots,K\}
 \cup \{p: p\le n\text{ and }p\text{ is prime}\}. \tag{12}
\]
By (11), every member of \(S\) lies in \(T_n\).

We next prove the crucial factorization assertion:

> Every integer \(m\) with \(1\le m\le n\) can be written as \(m=de\) with \(d,e\in S\).

Among all positive divisors of \(m\) that are at most \(K\), choose the largest and call it \(d\). This set of divisors is nonempty because \(1\mid m\) and \(1\le K\). Thus
\[
d\mid m,\qquad 1\le d\le K.
\]
Put
\[
e=m/d,
\]
so that \(m=de\). Since \(d\le K\), the number \(d\) belongs to the first part of \(S\). Also \(1\le e\le m\le n\).

If \(e\le K\), then \(e\) also lies in the first part of \(S\), and we are done. It remains to consider the case
\[
e>K. \tag{13}
\]
We claim that in this case \(e\) must be prime. Suppose instead that \(e\) is composite. Let \(q\) be its least prime divisor. Then
\[
q\mid e,
\qquad q^2\le e. \tag{14}
\]
The second assertion follows because \(e=q r\), where the least-prime-divisor property forces \(r\ge q\).

Since \(q\mid e\), the number \(dq\) divides \(de=m\). Moreover,
\[
dq>K. \tag{15}
\]
For if \(dq\le K\), then \(dq\) would be a divisor of \(m\) no larger than \(K\), but it would be strictly larger than \(d\), because \(q\ge2\). This contradicts the maximal choice of \(d\).

As all quantities are integers, (15) gives \(K+1\le dq\). Squaring and using (14) yields
\[
(K+1)^2\le(dq)^2=d^2q^2
 \le d^2e=d(de)=dm\le dn. \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, (13) gives \(K+1\le e\), and therefore
\[
d(K+1)\le de=m\le n. \tag{17}
\]
Multiplying (16) by \(K+1\), and then using (17), gives
\[
(K+1)^3
 \le (K+1)dn
 =n\,d(K+1)
 \le n^2. \tag{18}
\]
But (10) says \(n^2\le K^3\), whereas \((K+1)^3>K^3\). This contradicts (18). Hence \(e\) cannot be composite, so it is prime. Since also \(e\le n\), it belongs to the second part of \(S\).

Thus in every case \(m=de\) with \(d,e\in S\). We have proved
\[
T_n\subseteq S\cdot S. \tag{19}
\]
Together with \(S\subseteq T_n\), this says that \(S\) is an admissible set in the definition of \(a(n)\). Consequently
\[
a(n)\le |S|. \tag{20}
\]

### 3. Bounding the cardinality

The two pieces in (12) need not be disjoint, but the cardinality of their union is at most the sum of their cardinalities. Hence
\[
|S|\le K+\pi(n). \tag{21}
\]
It remains to bound \(K\). By (1),
\[
n^2\le8\bigl(\pi(n)+1\bigr)^3
 =\bigl(2(\pi(n)+1)\bigr)^3.
\]
Thus \(2(\pi(n)+1)\) is one of the integers whose cube is at least \(n^2\). Since \(K\) was chosen to be the least such integer,
\[
K\le2(\pi(n)+1). \tag{22}
\]
Combining (20), (21), and (22), we obtain
\[
a(n)
 \le K+\pi(n)
 \le2(\pi(n)+1)+\pi(n)
 =3\pi(n)+2.
\]
For \(n\ge2\), the prime \(2\) is counted, so \(\pi(n)\ge1\), and therefore \(2\le2\pi(n)\). It follows that
\[
a(n)\le3\pi(n)+2\le5\pi(n). \tag{23}
\]

Finally, \(\pi(n)>0\) for every \(n\ge2\), so division of (23) by \(\pi(n)\) gives
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le5\qquad(n\ge2).
\]
Thus the ratio \(a(n)/\pi(n)\) is bounded (indeed, uniformly bounded by \(5\)) as \(n\to\infty\).
